lines.en: What a headline chooses to shout and what it chooses to whisper tell you more than the story itself.
It is not only what the news reports that shapes opinion, but what it quietly leaves out.
Were the same event reported by two rival channels, you would hardly know it was the same event.
However neutral a report may sound, the choice of which expert to interview is already an opinion.
Not until you read the same story in three languages do you see how much of the news is framing.
It is said that the camera never lies, but it certainly chooses where to look.
What the algorithm shows you is not the world; it is the world most likely to keep you watching.
The study was widely reported as a breakthrough, though its authors had warned against exactly that word.
Little does the reader notice how the passive voice can hide who did what.
Rarely does a correction travel as far or as fast as the mistake it corrects.
What the photograph cropped out of the frame changed the story more than anything left inside it.
It is the repetition of a claim, not its truth, that makes it familiar enough to believe.
Were every reader to check one source before sharing, half the false news would die by morning.
Not until the interview is edited does the honest answer become a scandal.
However independent the channels may claim to be, their owners' names are printed in the registry for anyone to read.
